title: Meghan did not let her father see her children to protect them
description: Before today's allegations and the statement from the Duchess of Sussex there was not much at all between Meghan and her father.Quite when the duchess
body: Before today's allegations and the statement from the Duchess of Sussex there was not much at all between Meghan and her father.Quite when the duchess last saw her father Thomas isn't clear. By the time her engagement was announced in 2017, a once-close relationship had cooled.He had moved to Mexico following his retirement in the US and then, as he spoke freely to the media before and after her 2018 wedding, the relationship went into the deep freeze.He said she barely called as he underwent heart surgery, the duchess's people briefed that she had. Then they went silent as he complained in interview after interview that he no longer saw his daughter, had never met Harry nor, later, his grandchildren.Now Meghan has told us why.Thomas Markle gave the first, very large, hint that things would be different within weeks of the announcement of Meghan and Harry's wedding.Instead of accepting the embrace of the Palace - and the media silence that involves - he happily went rogue, giving comments, sometimes commentary, to various media outlets. He had what appeared to be a paid photoshoot whilst claiming that he was being harassed by the media, withdrawing from the wedding just days beforehand as he underwent heart surgery.There was no lack of drama.The interviews and comments never really stopped. Markle was a regular on some broadcast outlets, often complaining that he had no contact with his daughter and son-in-law or, later, his grandchildren.From Meghan came neither comment nor guidance as to why she had cut contact with the father with whom she had once been so close.And into that vacuum rushed theory and supposition - that Meghan was embarrassed by her father, that she and Harry felt their privacy had been compromised by him and so would no longer give him material to recycle, that the old man who was so close to the popular news outlets that tormented them was no longer part of the life they wanted to lead.Those theories became part of the case against Meghan;  that she would sacrifice anyone and anything - even her father - to protect her position and save herself from any embarrassment.That must have stung. Because today, without exactly using the word, she claimed vindication."I hope it can now be understood" she wrote. "That, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them."Meghan says she was informed of the allegations back in 2018. It is understood that it was after her marriage to Harry in May that year. Since then there has only been very limited contact between Meghan and her father - she wrote to him after he underwent surgery in the Philippines late last year.How much all of this changes the perception of Meghan is difficult to tell. Many people have made their minds up about Meghan and the saga with her father is only part of the tangled story of the duchess and the rest of the royal family.But her supporters will see vindication in the allegations - which have been denied by Thomas Markle - and the response that Meghan says she made when she first learned of them.

schema.headline: Meghan did not let her father see her children to protect them

title: Meghan says she was informed about 'disturbing allegations' against her father in 2018
description: The Duchess of Sussex has said she was informed about "disturbing allegations" about her estranged father in 2018.In a statement, Meghan said a letter
body: The Duchess of Sussex has said she was informed about "disturbing allegations" about her estranged father in 2018.In a statement, Meghan said a letter containing allegations against Thomas Markle was sent to the Metropolitan Police that year and subsequently shared with her.Her comments come after reports that images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to her father had been found at his former home in the Philippines.Thomas Markle, who is 82 and based in the US, denies possessing any such images.Commenting after the allegations, first reported by The Sun newspaper, external, the duchess said: "I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."She said that when she received the letter outlining allegations against her father, she was "given assurance that these were being investigated".She added she hoped it could be understood why she had kept her distance from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".This was "to protect them", Meghan said, adding that she had "trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families".She described the allegations as "more sickening than one could ever imagine" and said her "sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children". Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, alleged to The Sun that he had found child abuse images at his father's home in the Philippines and reported it to the police.The Undersecretary for the Philippines Department of Justice, Nicholas Ty, told the BBC that "the matter is currently being investigated" by an anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force in Cebu.Philippines Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla separately told the BBC that national police had secured Thomas Markle Snr's computer to conduct a comprehensive digital forensic examination. Investigators are currently analysing the data to determine the full scope and extent of his alleged criminal activities, with the minister saying it would take one week to get the forensic results.It is understood the Met has not and is not currently investigating Meghan's father. The force said it was carrying out an internal inquiry to confirm the Met's royal protection unit passed on the letter to the Duchess.The FBI said it was "aware of the allegations and will provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities. We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of US law."The BBC has contacted Thomas Markle Snr and the Metropolitan Police for comment.The allegations about Meghan's estranged father cast a new light on their complicated family relationships.The statement from the Duchess of Sussex says the sharing of information about her father happened in 2018 - the year in which she married Prince Harry.It is understood that Meghan first learnt about the allegations against her father after the wedding.Sources close to the Sussexes said Meghan could not speak publicly about the allegations when she first learned of them, in order to avoid jeopardising any future investigation. Speaking out could have resulted in legal action against her, the sources said. The claims add a fresh dimension to the questions about why Prince Harry and their children did not ever seem to have met Meghan's father - and why relations seemed to be so strained.With such question marks over her estranged father - and he has denied any wrongdoing - it also raises the issue of whether that played a part in the Sussexes' hurried return to the UK in late summer.However the Sussexes' spokesman has denied it was a factor in their decision to leave the US, where her father was living.The pair and their two children returned to the UK in August after six years in the US. They moved there after stepping back as senior royals in January 2020, meaning they no longer perform official royal duties or receive public funds.Meghan is the only child of Thomas Markle's marriage to her mother, Doria Ragland, but he has two other children - Samantha and Thomas Markle Jr - from an earlier marriage.The relationship between Meghan and her father, a former TV lighting director, broke down in the run-up to her wedding in 2018.At the time, Thomas Markle was found to have colluded with photographers, accepting payment to stage photographs of him preparing for the wedding. The resultant fall-out saw him pull out of his daughter's wedding, citing health problems. Meghan was instead walked down the aisle by King Charles III - then Prince of Wales.In 2025, Thomas Markle moved to the Philippines after a series of strokes. He is reportedly now living in a rehabilitation centre in Florida, where he is learning to walk again, after having a leg amputated during surgery in December 2025.Meghan sent a letter to her estranged father while he was in hospital in the Philippines after the procedure. title: Burnham suggests stocking up on tinned food and bottled water
description: The prime minister has advised people to stock up on tinned food and bottled water in order to be prepared for emergencies.With storms battering the U
body: The prime minister has advised people to stock up on tinned food and bottled water in order to be prepared for emergencies.With storms battering the UK, and in the wake of online disruption caused by a major security flaw, Andy Burnham said "unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common".The government has drawn up recommendations for households to have three days' worth of bottled water and tinned food to deal with a crisis such as a war, an online attack or a natural disaster.Burnham added: "It's not about panicking... It's about just taking sensible measures to have enough in the house to tide you over should there be a difficult situation."At Labour's conference last month, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner joked that her emergency box, external would include a bottle of wine.She said she'd include: "Mascara, concealer, I don't know, a bottle of Sauvignon Blanc, a tin of baked beans because you've gotta have some baked beans, and I like a good tin of custard as well so I think that'll keep me going for a while."Asked whether he agreed with her, Burnham told BBC Radio 5 Live's Matt Chorley: "Well, I'm not sure a bottle of wine is your best first port of call if you're in a slightly crisis situation, but it probably helps when you've done the hard work. "But I'll stick to the basics I think - I do like my beans, so I have plenty of those in the cupboard, and soup. "I think those are the kind of things that I would recommend people to have, as well as Twiglets, I'm not sure I can get by for too long without those."Last month, the National Audit Office (NAO) warned Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis and said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience.The chief executive of the Cold Chain Federation, which represents firms transporting temperature-controlled foods, also told the BBC the UK is being targeted by Russian cyber-hackers who "know that there are pinch points in the food supply system".Speaking at a wildfire resilience summit in Liverpool, Burnham denied the government had failed to properly prepare, saying: "No, we're having the conversation with people about being better prepared because we're living in a world where unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common."Obviously, weather events, and we're in a situation today where the UK is facing storms and obviously, we feel for the people without power in Cornwall right now."It is just having those supplies in the house to get you through those moments. So we are having that conversation about resilience."A checklist drawn up by the government recommends having nine litres of water per person – enough for three days – along with non-perishable food such as tinned meat and vegetables or dried fruit.The government suggests having an FM radio, either battery or wind-up. During a national crisis, the BBC would prioritise broadcasting news, as well as health and safety information. In the event of a severe power cut, FM radio will be the best way to receive these updates.The list also suggests hand sanitiser, wet wipes and toiletries, food for any pets, supplies for any babies, a torch, blankets, a charged power bank for devices, cash in case payment systems collapse, a first aid kit and copies of important documents.Earlier, Treasury minister James Murray told BBC Breakfast he has not yet followed the government's guidance on stockpiling supplies to prepare for a crisis.He said he had a stockpile of coffee, but pointed out that neighbouring countries including Ireland, France and the Netherlands had given the same guidance "for quite a long time".He added: "I'm not going to pretend I've followed all that advice myself yet."Speaking on the same programme, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said she was "stocked up for the week at any time".She said the previous Conservative government had issued similar advice on preparing for emergencies, but added: "What I'm more concerned about is that it doesn't look like [the government] are explaining what the risks we are under are, and what they are doing about the big things. "Families can stock up but what's going on with defence, the cyber attacks, the hybrid warfare? The money to look after the country has not been forthcoming."

schema.headline: Burnham suggests stocking up on tinned food and bottled water

title: Vincent Kompany: Bayern Munich manager taken to hospital after collapsing
description: Bayern Munich manager Vincent Kompany was taken to hospital after collapsing as he watched the club's second team train on Friday.The 40-year-old had
body: Bayern Munich manager Vincent Kompany was taken to hospital after collapsing as he watched the club's second team train on Friday.The 40-year-old had been unwell with a virus and missed the pre-match news conference on Tuesday prior to Bayern's Champions League game against Arsenal.The former Manchester City and Belgium defender was subsequently on the touchline for the match on Wednesday.Reports in Germany say Kompany is in a stable condition in hospital."Vincent Kompany required medical attention after collapsing during an FC Bayern reserve team training session on Friday," said a statement from the Bundesliga club., external "The first-team head coach was watching the second string's session. "Kompany is undergoing thorough examinations in hospital and will remain under medical care. "His coaching staff will oversee training and match activities until further notice."Bayern's next game is against Freiburg in the German top flight on Sunday."Vincent Kompany's health is our top priority. We at FC Bayern will do everything we can to ensure his speedy recovery," said Bayern sporting director Max Eberl."Vinnie is receiving all the necessary medical care and support, and all the time he needs. "His coaching team, in whom we have complete confidence, will take over his duties. All of us at FC Bayern wish Vinnie a speedy recovery."Aaron Danks, one of Kompany's assistants, took the pre-match news conference for Bayern before the Arsenal game.German football journalist Taufig Khalil told BBC Radio 5 Live that Kompany had been "suffering with the virus for about a week".He added: "The thing started last weekend on Saturday against Leipzig, and that's the first time we saw Vincent Kompany [when] he didn't look very well. "He didn't do the press conference after, and Max Eberl told us that he's suffering with a virus."Everybody was really surprised that Vincent Kompany was standing there with his black jacket in the pouring rain of Munich on Wednesday night against Arsenal. Everybody expected Aaron Danks to be there. "The problem was that maybe you couldn't bench Vincent Kompany, the game was too important for him."Bayern Munich just told us that he's in stable conditions. There was a helicopter involved in the whole thing, which landed on the training ground at Bayern Munich, but he was not brought into the hospital by helicopter. They brought him with a medical car and he will be now there."Kompany left his role as Burnley manager to take over at Bayern in May 2024, succeeding current England manager Thomas Tuchel.He had won the Championship with Burnley in 2022-23 and, despite the Clarets being relegated from the Premier League under him the following season, Kompany was appointed by the Bundesliga club.He has led Bayern to the German top-flight title in the past two seasons and reached the 2025-26 Champions League semi-finals before being beaten by eventual winners Paris St-Germain.Kompany spent 11 years at Manchester City as a player, winning four Premier League titles, two FA Cups and four League Cups.  "Everyone at Manchester City is wishing a speedy recovery to our former captain and club legend, Vincent Kompany," said City in a post on social media. "Get well soon, Vinny.""Everyone here at Burnley FC sends our best wishes to Vincent and we wish him a speedy recovery," said a Burnley statement.

schema.headline: Vincent Kompany: Bayern Munich manager taken to hospital after collapsing

title: Bodycam clip released in fatal police shooting of Mississippi one-year-old
description: Mississippi authorities have released body camera footage showing how a toddler was fatally shot by a police officer responding to a report of shoplif
body: Mississippi authorities have released body camera footage showing how a toddler was fatally shot by a police officer responding to a report of shoplifting in a Walmart car park.Kohen Wiley, aged one, was on his mother's lap in a moving car when officers surrounded the vehicle in the city of Senatobia on 14 June.The state's attorney general found the policeman was justified in using force, and the officer's lawyer argued in a statement to the BBC that the driver was attempting to kill law enforcement.The child's family disputes that the shooting was justified. Their lawyer, Ben Crump, has called the police response "excessive from the very start".Crump said an allegation of shoplifting "does not warrant the death" of a child.Kohen Wiley was riding in the vehicle with his mother, Vellesiya Wiley, and another woman at the time of the incident.Senatobia Mayor Greg Graves confirmed to the BBC's US partner CBS that Hunter Foster, the officer who opened fire, had resigned.The Senatobia Police Department did not immediately respond to the BBC's requests for confirmation.The footage released by Mississippi authorities on Thursday shows a first-person perspective of the officer who opened fire.After being told by a staff member that suspected shoplifters were getting away, five law enforcement officers run towards the car with guns drawn.The vehicle reverses, crashing into a parked car, before pulling forwards.The officer wearing the body camera raises his gun and aims it at the moving vehicle as he runs closer, shouting: "Stop!"As the car closely passes the officer, he fires his gun, shattering the passenger-side window.Four gunshots can be heard, as police command the driver to stop. The car continues to drive off slowly through the car park.CCTV video from the storefront appears to show that at the moment the policeman opens fire, another officer is standing near the front of the moving vehicle."The driver of the vehicle was attempting to kill those 5 officers," Martin Zummach, an attorney representing the officer, said in a statement to the BBC, adding that his client "had no choice but to discharge his weapon"."We are very sad for the loss of life," Zummach said. "But the outcome of the investigation was not only expected, but it was overdue."The child's mother, Wiley, has denied she and her friend stole nappies from the store. No charges have been filed against them.The boy's death has sparked protests and vigils in Mississippi.At a news conference, relatives demanded accountability."After what I've seen today, I'm having a difficult time understanding the word, 'justified,' said LaSandra Williams, Kohen Wiley's grandmother.

schema.headline: Bodycam clip released in fatal police shooting of Mississippi one-year-old

title: GP says she was forced out of job after raising concerns about gender treatment
description: A doctor who raised concerns about the treatment of children questioning their gender has told the BBC she was accused of transphobia, bullied and har
body: A doctor who raised concerns about the treatment of children questioning their gender has told the BBC she was accused of transphobia, bullied and harassed out of her child protection job in the NHS.Dr Sarah Redvers, who was a named safeguarding GP, said she faced a brutal investigation after she passed on complaints brought to her by other doctors.Speaking publicly for the first time, Redvers said she felt she was "silenced" for doing her job after questioning whether another GP was appropriately assessing the needs of young people who were distressed about their gender identity.She has brought a claim of constructive dismissal against the NHS Sussex Integrated Care Board (ICB), which managed health services in the county, and Adam Doyle, who was the ICB's chief executive until 2025.Redvers told a three-week employment tribunal hearing that she felt the focus on investigating her meant issues of patient safety had been sidelined."I was just bewildered really that the medical and safeguarding issues were completely lost," she said. "It's really risky," she told the BBC.NHS Surrey and Sussex said: "We recognise that some employment processes should have been handled differently." They have apologised to Redvers.In June 2026, nearly six years after she first raised concerns, a separate NHS safety investigation found that dozens of children, some as young as 13, had been inappropriately prescribed drugs at the WellBN practice, the clinic where the other doctor worked.The report said 78 children had potentially been harmed after puberty-blocking drugs and cross sex hormones were prescribed to them without proper checks.The report said it was in response to a drug review carried out in autumn 2024, not to the concerns first raised by Redvers years earlier.NHS England said: "It is totally unacceptable young people were put at risk of harm because some practitioners at the WellBN practice provided care they were not commissioned to deliver by the NHS.""To read about a medical scandal knowing it could have been stopped was upsetting," said Redvers, "because concerns were raised appropriately and leaders knew about it".Redvers, who has many years of experience working with vulnerable groups, was a named safeguarding GP for Sussex, which meant other doctors who had safety concerns about patients could turn to her for advice and help.The tribunal heard that in July 2020, a doctor got in touch because she was worried about a patient who had gone to an online clinic which was registered overseas. It wanted the GP to take over prescribing testosterone to a vulnerable 18-year-old female, who was distressed about her gender. The doctor was also given advice on such prescriptions by a Brighton GP, Dr Sam Hall."The concerns to me were that Hall was recommending treatment for patients that he hadn't assessed, that he hadn't met, and that other GPs were uncomfortable with prescribing," Redvers said.Redvers spoke to NHS England (NHSE) and was advised to make the complaint as a whistleblower.It was investigated and NHSE said it was satisfied with Hall's practice.Over the following months several other GPs voiced their concerns to Redvers about the quality of assessments, the prescription of puberty blocking drugs and cross sex hormones, and the lack of specialist supervision at the WellBN clinic, where Hall was based.Again, the NHS investigated her concerns. She said she was also told by the investigator that there was a "general worry" that there "would be allegations of transphobia."Hall, who is a trans man and was born female, qualified as a GP in 2019 and is known as a campaigner for transgender rights in Brighton.Publicly, he had said that his own pain had shown him the importance of "affirmative care" - support for a patient in a way which accepts rather than challenges their preferred gender and treatment decisions follow from that.He was also working with the NHS locally on setting up a Trans Health hub and with a Brighton trans support charity called The Clare Project.The second NHS investigation considered "the full scope" of Hall's work and concluded there was no cause for concern. It also said there was "one colleague whose persistent interest in the issue appeared disproportionate." Redvers took that to mean her.The concerns she said she and others were raising were about the quality of care being provided, and whether it had the necessary medical evidence to underpin it, not her views on gender."It's about medical assessment and treatment of patients, which is something we have to get right, particularly in this complex group of vulnerable patients," she said.She said she viewed any suggestion of transphobia as "appalling," and it was "dangerous" that such claims were obscuring the medical and safeguarding issues she was raising.In 2021, whilst waiting for the outcome of the second investigation and prompted by a concern raised by local mental health services about the care of a vulnerable 15-year-old, Redvers referred Hall to the medical regulator, the GMC.Hall emailed Adam Doyle, then CEO of NHS Sussex, directly to complain."I am being victimised here, and I need proper protection from this individual and their repeated attempts to disrupt my career" he said.Although Doyle at first denied to the tribunal he knew Hall before this, it emerged during the tribunal that he had previously had a number of mentoring meetings with the GP.The GMC investigation was not taken forward. However, the NHS launched an investigation into Redvers, bringing in an external investigator.The tribunal heard she was called to what she described as a "brutal" four-hour interrogation."It was oppressive, very upsetting. I didn't feel I had the chance at all to explain what had happened," she said.  "I broke down at one point".She said she was off sick for several months as a result and received treatment for trauma.Other colleagues who were interviewed as part of the investigation into Redvers also complained about the process and the NHS upheld most of their complaints.The investigation concluded the CEO and trust should apologise to Redvers.It also warned that Redvers' treatment would have a "broader negative impact" on the willingness of staff to raise concerns.In 2023, a year after the grievance outcome, when a trans campaigner suggested in an NHS meeting that she was transphobic, Redvers told the tribunal she felt the NHS did not do enough to support her. She felt she had no choice but to leave her job as a safeguarding GP."I just felt there's no way I could carry on working in this organisation," she told the BBC.At about that time, a group of parents, school governors and social workers began raising concerns about WellBn and Hall.The co-founder of campaign group PSHE Brighton, Rachel Cashman, said: "It is a travesty that Sarah Redvers was punished for doing her job safeguarding and expecting the best standards of care for gender distressed children."Redvers is now waiting for the outcome of her employment tribunal. She may not get the judgment for several months. She described what has happened as "personally and professionally difficult" and said the NHS "needs to remember that patients come first" and it should "listen to staff who raise legitimate concerns."In a statement NHS Surrey and Sussex said: "We engaged professionally and supportively with the Employment Tribunal.  We recognise that some employment processes should have been handled differently and have apologised whilst Dr Redvers was employed with us, before, and during the hearings.  We await the findings of the tribunal to make any further comment."NHS England said: "When concerns about prescribing practices by an individual GP were escalated to NHS England national directors in 2023, they met directly with an affected family and asked regional professional standards leads to undertake formal investigations."Wider concerns were subsequently identified, and the WellBN practice was asked to stop providing a specialised prescribing service. Further new information led to NHS England and NHS Sussex initiating an independent patient safety investigation in 2025."Dr Sam Hall and WellBN have been contacted for comment.In response to the investigation report in June, WellBN said it recognised "the seriousness and sensitivity of the matters raised" and that its priority remained providing "compassionate, safe and effective care for all patients".

schema.headline: GP says she was forced out of job after raising concerns about gender treatment

title: 'It's been relentless' say IT workers on frontline of PHP cyber security scramble
description: Microsoft boss Satya Nadella says he has not seen anything like the PHP emergency "in a long, long time".Referencing the ongoing global efforts to fix
body: Microsoft boss Satya Nadella says he has not seen anything like the PHP emergency "in a long, long time".Referencing the ongoing global efforts to fix the critical cyber-security flaw in millions of websites, he told a conference "it was a long day and a long night, I know, for all the IT and security folks".Other IT and cyber experts have told the BBC about their struggles in the last 48 hours, whose stories give us an insight into what it is like at the coalface of a major cyber emergency. But also highlight how misinformation and panic has made things a lot worse."It's been relentless," says UK-based system administrator Adam Mudd.He said he had never had so many messages from people who were worried about their websites."The biggest challenge has been juggling clients who want their sites taken offline as a precaution, while trying to coordinate updates and fixes across countless different setups," he said. "Sometimes it takes me longer to take a website down than to fix the PHP problem."PHP is a very popular programming language which powers millions of websites.But two critical flaws were found with the system that led to the emergency response, with national cyber-security authorities urging IT teams to download a security fix urgently or take websites and servers offline.Mudd says since then he has been under enormous pressure and has lost a huge amount of sleep - working early and not finishing until 22:30 BST to secure his customers' systems.In Mauritius, IT administrator Loganaden Velvindron said he too was flat out since his team realised just how much software relies on PHP."Many versions of php running are completely end-of-life, so we are having to rebuilding web apps and change code in some cases," he said.He said part of the problem was the announcement about the security vulnerabilities in PHP came as a surprise, without much time to prepare for action.Jon Jones, Technical director for a digital advertising company, was also spurred into action by the alerts."Seeing the warning drop was definitely eye-opening and a new experience we've not dealt with before," he said."But, in a way, it was exciting feeling like a bit of a Hollywood action scene."The PHP Foundation, which manages the programming language, released its software fix and there was a scramble for people to download it.Jones said it felt like "the race was on" when the patch launched at 15:00 BST on Wednesday."It was also a bit nerve-racking as anyone who has applied software updates before would know, there's always a chance than an update can cause other issues," he said.The rush came as someone had leaked details of the PHP flaw early - and it was heavily rumoured that cyber-criminals were already trying to carry out attacks.But cyber experts are also now questioning whether or not those rumours were real."We were flooded with rubbish intel about hackers being out there actively with working Proof of Concept (PoC) methods," said UK cyber expert Daniel Card.He said he also been flat out since Tuesday when the rumours of PHP hacks began circulating."This isn't the first time we've had a situation like this but it feels like it's been on another dimension," he said.He agreed that on paper the PHP vulnerabilities were very serious and should be taken seriously, but he and many others are frustrated with the misinformation about hackers being on the loose.As well as the alerts from government agencies - even the Prime Minister of Japan - cyber-security companies also made errors which didn't help.One major firm in this space issued warnings saying hackers had a working PoC - only to have to retract it.In spite of warnings from Cloudflare and AWS that "millions of hacking attempts" had been made every hour, there is also no evidence of large scale data breaches or cyber-attacks.It is true that hackers have been seen to use AI to attempt to build attack methods, but none of them seem to be working at scale at the moment - something that may well change soon.AI was also used to find the PHP flaws which had been hidden from human researchers for decades.The IT workers we spoke to all agreed that these kinds of serious flaws were going to be uncovered more frequently now that AI tools had become so good at hacking.But some in the industry are concerned about how people were told about the critical vulnerabilities in PHP, as they fear improvements in AI will throw up more incidents like it."We're going to find scary vulnerabilities with the amazing capabilities that OpenAI and Anthropic are bringing online, but we need to calibrate the messaging," posted Mark Maunder, founder of Wordfence - a Wordpress security tool.He said there was a risk of "alert fatigue" which could be a big problem if a fully exploitable and serious vulnerability arose.

schema.headline: 'It's been relentless' say IT workers on frontline of PHP cyber security scramble

title: Oil spill washes up on UAE beaches after tanker strike
description: ByThomas Copeland, Mark Poynting and Tom SpencerBBC VerifyAn oil spill from a tanker attacked near the Strait of Hormuz is spreading along the United
body: ByThomas Copeland, Mark Poynting and Tom SpencerBBC VerifyAn oil spill from a tanker attacked near the Strait of Hormuz is spreading along the United Arab Emirates (UAE) coastline, forcing the closure of some beaches and coastal areas.Satellite images from Monday show the beginnings of the oil spill from a ship matching the location and dimensions of Gem No.2, which was damaged between 9 and 10 October during a record surge of vessel strikes by Iran.The slick of oil had spread more than 35km (22 miles) from the tanker by Wednesday, the satellite imagery showed.UAE authorities said on Thursday that the incident is affecting beaches near the northern city of Umm Al Quwain and verified video from Friday shows the oil washing ashore, colouring the water black.The UAE's Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Thursday that it "immediately began containment" in order to "limit environmental impacts".Prof Steve Widdicombe, director of Sharjah Marine Science Research Centre in the UAE, told BBC Verify it was "inevitable that there will be an impact", but researchers caution it is too soon to assess extent of the damage.Initially a much smaller oil leak could be seen emerging from the ship on 19 October.But the slick appears to have rapidly spread over two days, according to radar satellite imagery reviewed by BBC Verify and intelligence firm MAIAR.Oil spills can cause immediate deaths of marine animals and other organisms, for example by physically trapping turtles, smothering the feathers of seabirds or damaging the gills of fish.They can also cause longer-lasting damage, Prof Widdicombe said, if species remain exposed to toxic compounds from the oil which could impact their ability to reproduce.Researchers have cautioned the environmental impact at this stage is very uncertain, as it depends on factors including the volume and type of oil spilled, how quickly it evaporates or breaks down and the effectiveness of the clean-up operation.But the spill does extend towards Siniyah and Khor Al Beidah islands, a globally recognised Key Biodiversity Area containing habitats like corals, seagrasses and saltmarshes, as well as species including green turtles and the critically endangered Halavi guitarfish.The proximity of the spill to this area is the "most concerning environmental angle", according to Eoghan Darbyshire, a scientist at the Conflict and Environment Observatory.Tanker hit 14 days agoBBC Verify analysis of the dimensions and location of the ship indicate they match a crude oil tanker called Gem No.2.Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard reported the Panama-flagged tanker was "struck by an unknown projectile" on 9 October, just north of the town of Al Jazeera Al Hamra, causing a fire on board that was later extinguished.Verified footage first posted on social media on 10 October showed the crew running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rose over the ship.Iranian state media shared footage of a ship matching Gem No.2 which appeared to show the vessel on fire with burning oil spilling into the sea.The ship had been attempting to exit the Strait of Hormuz via an "unauthorized and dangerous route", according to state media.All 22 Indian crew members were rescued, the Indian consulate in Dubai said on 11 October.Gem No.2 is one of a record number of ships that reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz at the start of October.Security experts told BBC Verify this was part of an Iranian effort to assert greater control over the strait, in response to the US military successfully escorting more vessels through the vital shipping lane.Tankers and other commercial vessels have come under attack from both Iranian and US forces in and around the Strait of Hormuz amid the conflict between the two countries.Another major oil slick washed up on the shores of Iran's Qeshm Island in August, which experts said threatened wildlife, protected ecosystems and fishing communities.Additional reporting by Charlotte Green

title: Jordan church shooting leaves seven dead, officials say
description: Seven people have been killed in an attack on a funeral in central Jordan, officials have said.At least 34 others were injured as gunmen opened fire o
body: Seven people have been killed in an attack on a funeral in central Jordan, officials have said.At least 34 others were injured as gunmen opened fire on a church in Hmoud, in the Karak governorate on Friday.The unidentified gunmen are reported to have arrived in a car, entered the church and opened fire before fleeing. No-one has admitted carrying out the attack.In a news conference, Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya said authorities were working to apprehend the perpetrators which he described as a "group of extremists".Jordan's King Abdullah II, said the authorities would "confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties".Initial reports indicated seven people had been killed in the attack. A government spokesperson later said six people had died, before officials again revised the death toll to seven.CCTV footage, verified by the BBC, appears to shows three gunmen making their way from a road toward the church.Two of the attackers are seen making their way on to what appears to be a vehicle entrance to the church grounds, before retreating briefly and returning with a third man. All three appear to be armed with handguns.Separate footage believed to be from the aftermath of the attack appears to show several dead and wounded bodies on the ground amid some chaotic scenes.Witnesses have described scenes of panic inside the church as people threw themselves under pews searching for cover, moving away from the windows.Prayers and screams could be heard throughout the building as some tried to flee.Khalid al-Mdanat was at the church and told BBC Arabic the attack lasted around 15 minutes with "people trying to flee while the shooting was still active"."People began pushing and throwing themselves to the ground," he said."Some were taking cover, some were cradling the dead, others were holding their sons close, some were grabbing their children and fleeing, while others were holding onto their friends who were with them at the church."He said the gunmen left through the church doors and fled in a pickup truck "firing as they went".Another witness said: "I heard something as if a war had just started."I thought it was an electrical short circuit. I looked, people lying on the ground, wounded. The scene was catastrophic."A woman in the church said explosions rang out seconds after a prayer."The sound of machine guns started, and the sound of glass. We began to realise that something was happening."People started screaming. The witness described how the situation "continued to escalate for 10 continuous minutes". Once she ran out the church she said "bodies were all in the courtyards".Al-Faraya has described the incident as "painful and horrific" and "unparalleled in the history of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan".There was a heavy security presence at the entrance to a hospital treating people injured in the incident in Karak, amid an atmosphere charged with anger among residents of the governorate, particularly the families of those injured and killed.Many looked distressed as roads were closed around the facility and people were forced to park their cars and continue on foot.Security measures were also tightened ahead of the visit by King Abdullah II to check on the injured.The atmosphere around the hospital remained tense as the sound of crying and shouting was heard as families mourned their loved ones.Many people appear shocked, frightened and angry. Some expressed frustration at what they described as "a failure to take a tougher approach towards terrorists".Karak has a sizeable Christian community in the majority-Muslim Jordan.Such violence is rare in the country, but deadly attacks have been carried out in the past.Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun, a Christian head of state, said the "heinous terrorist attack" on the church "violated the sanctity of death and funeral mourners, contradicts all religious and humanitarian values," according to Lebanese media.Additional reporting by Majdi Gousous, BBC Arabic.

schema.headline: Jordan church shooting leaves seven dead, officials say

title: Woman at centre of Cornell University rape inquiry in 'constant fear', lawyer says
description: The life of a woman who filed a lawsuit alleging she was drugged and raped at a Cornell University fraternity house has been completely upended, her l
body: The life of a woman who filed a lawsuit alleging she was drugged and raped at a Cornell University fraternity house has been completely upended, her lawyer has said. Speaking to the BBC ahead of a hearing in the civil case on Friday in New York, her lawyer Thomas Giuffra said: "She feels under fire."The woman, known anonymously as Jane Doe, is suing her former school and the fraternity over the alleged incident involving several men at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024.When the case went viral, a series of "I am Jane Doe" solidarity posts appeared, but  there was a separate campaign aimed at unmasking her and defending the men, who have all denied any wrongdoing. The men, who are also being sued by the woman, have not been charged with any crimes. With initial proceedings now under way in the civil case, Giuffra told the BBC that these last few weeks have been "a very hard time" for his client, who isn't doing a lot beyond "surviving".Her decision to sue was rooted in a desire for closure and to take power back, he said.Giufrra visited Jane Doe this week and found that she hadn't been sleeping well – relying on medication to get rest.Now in trauma therapy, he says she doesn't feel safe in her own home following malicious threats that were directed at her and her family.After her address was published online without her consent, someone called in a fake emergency that led to police in full tactical gear drawing assault rifles on her father, her friend and her brother at their family home."It's just constant fear," he said. He added that despite this her resolve hadn't been shaken and she remains determined to overhaul the university system at Cornell, and across the country, to protect survivors.Cornell University, after initially defending its disciplinary measures, acknowledged it fell short in its handling of Jane Doe's case.After facing intense pressure, the college's president announced that fraternity parties would be suspended until the end of the academic year to allow for a thorough review to determine whether and how they can safely continue. The school also said it would add sexual assault investigators to its police force.Giuffra, however, says he is surprised that Cornell has not reached out to him and believes they have been focused solely on "damage control". He says any agreement with Cornell to resolve the civil lawsuit will need to include "steps to ensure there are no more Jane Does" and if there are, that they are going to be supported.The BBC contacted Cornell for comment who directed us to the university's previous statements and comments on its internal investigation in 2024.New York's governor Kathy Hochul appointed a special prosecutor, New York's Attorney General Letitia James, to oversee a reopened investigation into whether criminal charges are warranted.Giuffra expects it will take a long time to do a proper investigation but is concerned that they will be going after evidence that is now "stale"."A lot of the communication was on Snapchat, Snapchat goes away," he told the BBC. "The best time to get evidence is around the time of the crime and that just didn't happen."However, Giuffra believes he can win the civil case against the university, the men and others, where the burden of proof is lower than a criminal case. Civil cases require a preponderance of the evidence, that it's more likely than not it happened, while criminal cases require proof beyond a reasonable doubt. Recent high profile cases have shown the way juries evaluate consent can be unpredictable."I wouldn't have taken the case if I didn't think it was a strong case that I could win and get her some closure."

schema.headline: Woman at centre of Cornell University rape inquiry in 'constant fear', lawyer says

title: LIV Golf: Ian Poulter & Tyrrell Hatton are latest stars to leave breakaway tour
description: Englishmen Ian Poulter and Tyrrell Hatton are the latest star names to confirm they are quitting LIV Golf - leaving the breakaway tour's future lookin
body: Englishmen Ian Poulter and Tyrrell Hatton are the latest star names to confirm they are quitting LIV Golf - leaving the breakaway tour's future looking increasingly uncertain.Poulter joined LIV when it launched as a Saud Arabia-backed project in 2022, while Hatton signed up in 2024.But the pair have followed major champions Jon Rahm and Louis Oosthuizen in announcing their departures.Northern Ireland's Tom McKibbin has also said he will leave LIV and return to the DP World Tour. Saudi's Public Investment Fund withdrew its backing from LIV in April - having pumped in more than $5bn (£3.8bn) - leading to the league filing for bankruptcy protection in the United States last month.It has secured a possible $300m (£224m) in financing from BC Partners Credit to try to move forward with 'LIV 2.0', but only a handful of players have so far committed to the proposed competition in 2027.Poulter, 50, said he wants to help his two sons, Luke and Joshua, pursue professional careers, as well as develop his YouTube channel."I wanted everyone to hear it direct from me that I have decided to not move forward with being part of LIV 2.0," he wrote on his social media channels."Needless to say, it was a tough decision and one I thought about and discussed at length with my family and team."Ultimately, the opportunity to spend more time at home with my family, reduce international travel, focus on senior golf and have the opportunity to pursue other interests was something that I felt was right for me at this stage of my life and career."Hatton, 35, made a brief statement his Instagram account which confirmed his decision to leave the event."Wanted to confirm I will not be part of a LIV 2.0," he wrote."A big thank you to everyone for their continued support. I am excited for what the next chapter of my career holds."McKibbin, who joined LIV in January 2025, said in an Instagram post he had "decided not to sign with LIV Golf for its next chapter" and plans to play the full DP World Tour schedule in 2027."Joining LIV Golf was the right decision for me at the time, and I'm grateful for everything it has given me," the 23-year-old wrote."I've taken time to think about what's best for me and I am confident this is the right decision to help me achieve my goals."Former world number five Poulter was co-captain of the Majesticks team alongside fellow Englishman and Ryder Cup icon Lee Westwood, while Hatton and McKibbin were both part of Rahm's Legion XIII team.Westwood's future plans remain unclear.The decision of the English duo to leave came in the same week as 2010 Open champion Oosthuizen, who captained the Southern Guards GC team and said quitting was the "hardest decision" of his career.Last week, two-time major winner Rahm gave up a reported £75m owed to him by LIV after reaching a separation agreement.Abraham Ancer and David Puig are also leaving, while Sergio Garcia, Thomas Pieters, Tom McKibbin, Laurie Canter and Adrian Meronk appear unlikely to stay with LIV.Richard Bland, Cameron Tringale and Brendan Steele are three of the few players to commit to the second phase of the breakaway circuit.LIV's future could hinge on whether it can secure the signature of American superstar Bryson DeChambeau, who ESPN reported earlier this week "remains committed" to the league.In his statement, Poulter acknowledged LIV has "clearly divided opinion", but said he will be "forever proud" to be part of its founding group."Change is never easy and it's fair to say professional golf has experienced plenty of it over the last few years," he added."But I've always believed that change can create opportunity and ultimately lead to positive outcomes. "There will undoubtedly be more changes ahead, but I am confident the game will continue to grow, evolve, and deliver the very best for golf fans around the world."

schema.headline: LIV Golf: Ian Poulter & Tyrrell Hatton are latest stars to leave breakaway tour

title: Macron says deadly shooting near Paris is a 'racist terrorist attack'
description: French President Emmanuel Macron has labelled a gun attack in a Parisian suburb which killed one person and injured five others "a racist terrorist at
body: French President Emmanuel Macron has labelled a gun attack in a Parisian suburb which killed one person and injured five others "a racist terrorist attack".Macron said the attack was a "turning point in the life of our Republic and our nation" - the first time there has ever been a random racial killing like this.The attack unfolded over some 15 minutes with the attacker opening fire from his car - first in Trappes to the south-west of Paris, and then in nearby La Verrière - appearing to target people of migrant origin. He was subsequently arrested.Three of those injured, including a 12-year-old girl, remain in a serious condition.Visiting the scene of the attack in Trappes, Macron said people had been targeted for their skin colour or religion and urged the public not to give an inch in the face of what he called "ideologies taking root".The exact motive remains unclear, but the National Anti-Terrorist Prosecutor's Office (PNAT) said the incident appeared to be "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise".The suspect has been named in French media as Kevin T who, according to PNAT, had four previous convictions which had been "automatically expunged".The 39-year-old was known to police but not to France's intelligence services, local media report.He was not on a list of individuals considered to be a serious threat to French security, the national anti-terrorism prosecutor's office told BFMTV.A member of the suspect's "immediate family circle" was also taken into custody on Friday, it added.The Mayor of Trappes, Ali Rabeh, said that "an individual fired shots from his vehicle at several people he encountered" on Friday morning.The gunman drove through several neighbourhoods in a grey Renault Clio, according to witnesses. Rabeh said he had  "fired randomly" with the seeming intent of causing "as many casualties as possible... he wanted to cause carnage", he said.The mayor said people had been targeted at a petrol station, a medical centre and a playground in Trappes before the attacker had driven on to nearby La Verrière.A police union official said the suspect had been detained in La Verrière on the main N10 road that runs through the town.

schema.headline: Macron says deadly shooting near Paris is a 'racist terrorist attack'

title: White House says Melania Trump brokers truce for Ukraine city 'on brink of disaster'
description: Image source, Ksenia ArkhipovaImage caption, These residents were able to get out of Oleshky in spring this yearByJaroslav Lukiv and Bernd Debusmann J
body: Image source, Ksenia ArkhipovaImage caption, These residents were able to get out of Oleshky in spring this yearByJaroslav Lukiv and Bernd Debusmann JrWhite House reporterUpdated 3 hours agoUS First Lady Melania Trump has "successfully secured" a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, the White House has said.It said the truce in the "front-line war city on the brink of disaster" without medicine, food and clean water would begin on 29 October.Ukraine and Russia confirmed the deal was agreed to evacuate residents and deliver aid. They both said their forces would stop firing at 02:00 GMT on 27 October.Oleshky was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Trapped between Ukrainian positions across the Dnipro River and Russian forces to the east, residents have recently resorted to eating garden weeds to survive.Figure caption, Trump: First lady's 'initiative' led to truce for Ukraine cityThe White House statement said Melania Trump and one of her representatives had worked "directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localised ceasefire"."Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," she is quoted as saying."Residents who wish to evacuate will receive co-ordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine."Melania Trump added that Oleshky residents "have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks" and that "without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible".The statement did not say how long the ceasefire would be in place for.Davyd Arakhamia, a Ukrainian MP who heads President Volodymyr Zelensky's party in parliament, later said "an operation to unblock the settlement of Oleshky and its surroundings will begin in the near future"."To achieve this goal, a ceasefire will be achieved in the near future, as announced by the First Lady of the United States, Melania Trump," he said.In Russia, President Vladimir Putin's spokesman confirmed that, "those who wish to do so will be able to leave this settlement".Image source, Ksenia ArkhipovaImage caption, Oleshky has been without gas or electricity since 2023, so residents have had to find other solutionsLast month, some of the remaining Oleshky residents told the BBC harrowing accounts of how they were surviving in the city that was being constantly shelled and cut off from food and water.They said that children remaining in wider Oleshky were suffering from malnutrition, a lack of medical services and were "degrading" without access to education.Many also told the BBC there was only one hospital partially operational, opening a few days a week to perform critical amputations.The local population was living under a "full blockade" by Russian forces, according to Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha.Ukraine says it has attempted to deliver supplies to the area but has not had success in recent months.The Kremlin in September acknowledged that Oleshky was facing "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv.Oleshky was home to 24,000 people before Russia's full-scale invasion. Now  Ukraine estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children.It is also one of a number of settlements where thousands of people lost their homes to a massive flooding caused by the collapse of Nova Khakovka Dam in 2023. Ukraine and its allies accused Russia of blowing up the dam, while Russia blamed Ukraine.Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, Melania Trump worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to agree the ceasefire, the White House said.While the US first lady is relatively lower profile than some of her predecessors - and only occasionally seen at White House events - she has become involved in addressing humanitarian issues stemming from the Russia-Ukraine war.In August 2025, Melania Trump penned a letter to Putin, telling him it was "time to protect children and future generations worldwide".Although she did not mention Ukraine by name, just days later at the White House Zelensky handed over a letter from his wife Olena, thanking her for her efforts on children.In a rare public appearance in October the same year, the US first lady said that Putin had answered directly in writing and that her representatives were working with the Russian president's team to repatriate Ukrainian children from Russia and vice versa.Some 34 children have reportedly been returned since 2025, including five this July.According to US President Donald Trump, his wife has also privately expressed scepticism about Putin and his desire to achieve peace."I'd get home, I'd say, 'First lady, I had the most wonderful talk with Vladimir. I think we're finished'," Trump said in July last year."And then I'll turn on the television, or she'll say to me one time, 'Wow, that's strange because they just bombed a nursing home.'"Additional reporting by Olga Malchevska

schema.headline: White House says Melania Trump brokers truce for Ukraine city 'on brink of disaster'

title: Israeli forces begin demolishing Palestinian buildings in Hebron after two Israeli soldiers shot dead
description: The incident has already begun to influence the ongoing election campaign, with Netanyahu - who has built his campaign on the promise of security - sa
body: The incident has already begun to influence the ongoing election campaign, with Netanyahu - who has built his campaign on the promise of security - saying that his Likud party would cancel campaign events which had been set for Friday morning. Speaking later from the scene, Netanyahu said that the military would "demolish this place and completely transform it," referring to the Hebron neighbourhood where the attackers are said to have come from. It is common for Israeli forces to demolish the homes of Palestinians who are suspected of carrying out attacks on Israelis - a practice Israeli rights groups have criticised as collective punishment. Netanyahu likened his plans to previous operations in West Bank refugee camps where residential buildings were demolished and thousands were displaced. He also said he had reviewed plans for the largest military operation in the West Bank in decades - though did not say when it could be carried out. He added that he had imposed cordons around the city of Hebron - which has around 200,000 residents - and the nearby city of Halhul. Netanyahu's far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for Israel to launch a campaign in the West Bank "exactly like in Gaza or Lebanon," while far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir called for Israel to dismantle the Palestinian Authority. On Thursday, Foreign Minister Israel Katz accused opposition leaders of undermining the government by criticising Netanyahu's warnings of an attack ahead of the election, saying they would be "responsible" for any future attack on the country.Opposition chiefs, including frontrunner Gadi Eisenkot and former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, offered their condolences to the families of the killed troops and praised those who killed the attackers.The Israeli military said it had found a large quantity of ammunition in the attackers' vehicle, and that they believe the gunmen had intended to carry out a much larger attack on the nearby Route 35, but ran into the checkpoint - so instead decided to open fire there. At least 96 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank since the start of the year, according to the UN. Four Israelis, both security forces and civilians, have been killed by Palestinians there over the same period, the UN says - not including those killed in Friday's attack.

schema.headline: Israeli forces begin demolishing Palestinian buildings in Hebron after two Israeli soldiers shot dead
